Where the name of any person appears on any document in respect of which any person is charged with an offence under sub-section (1) or on any other document used or distributed in connection with that document it may, until the contrary is proved, be presumed that that person caused the document to be made.
Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 490: Breach of contract of service during voyage or journey. Repealed by the Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (3 of 1925), S. 2 and Sch.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 491: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless persons Whoever, being bound by a lawful contract to attend on or to supply the wants of any person who, by reason of youth, or of unsoundness of mind, or of a disease or bodily weakness, is helpless or incapable of providing for his own safety or of supplying his own wants, voluntarily omits so to do, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three months, or with fine which may extend to two hundred rupees, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 492: Breach of contract to serve at distant place to which servant is conveyed at master Repealed by the Workmen's Breach of Contract (Repealing) Act, 1925 (3 of 1925), S. 2 and Sch.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 493: Cohabitation caused by a man deceitfully inducing a belief of lawful marriage Every man who by deceit causes any woman who is not lawfully married to him to believe that she is lawfully married to him and to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him in that belief, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 494: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 495: Same offence with concealment of former marriage from person with whom subsequent marriage is contracted Whoever commits the offence defined in the last preceding section having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 496: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage Whoever, dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, goes through the ceremony of being married, knowing that he is not thereby lawfully married, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 497: Adultery Whoever has sexual intercourse with a person who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of another man, without the consent or connivance of that man, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, is guilty of the offence of adultery, and shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, or with fine, or with both. In such case the wife shall not be punishable as an abettor.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 498: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman Whoever takes or entices away any woman who is and whom he knows or has reason to believe to be the wife of any other man, from that man, or from any person having the care of her on behalf of that man, with intent that she may have illicit intercourse with any person, or conceals or detains with that intent any such woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 498A: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty Whoever, being the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman, subjects such woman to cruelty shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 499: Defamation Whoever by words either spoken or intended to be read, or by signs or by visible representations, makes or publishes any imputation concerning any person intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that such imputation will harm, the reputation of such person, is said, except in the cases hereinafter excepted, to defame that person.
Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 500: Punishment for defamation Whoever defames another shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 501: Printing or engraving matter known to be defamatory Whoever prints or engraves any matter, knowing or having good reason to believe that such matter is defamatory of any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 502: Sale of printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter Whoever sells or offers for sale any printed or engraved substance containing defamatory matter, knowing that it contains such matter, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 503: Criminal intimidation Whoever threatens another with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 504: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of the peace Whoever intentionally insults, and thereby gives provocation to any person, intending or knowing it to be likely that such provocation will cause him to break the public peace, or to commit any other offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 505: Statements conducing public mischief Whoever commits an offence specified in sub-section (2) in any place of worship or in any assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies, shall be punished with imprisonment which may extend to five years and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 506: Punishment for criminal intimidation Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both;

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 507: Criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication, or having taken precaution to conceal the name or abode of the person from whom the threat comes, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, in addition to the punishment provided for the offence by the last preceding section.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 508: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of the Divine displeasure Whoever voluntarily causes or attempts to cause any person to do anything which that person is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do anything which he is legally entitled to do, by inducing or attempting to induce that person to believe that he or any person in whom he is interested will become or will be rendered by some act of the offender an object of Divine displeasure if he does not do the thing which it is the object of the offender to cause him to do, or if he does the thing which it is the object of the offender to cause him to omit, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 509: Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman Whoever, intending to insult the modesty of any woman, utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits any object, intending that such word or sound shall be heard, or that such gesture or object shall be seen, by such woman, or intrudes upon the privacy of such woman, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also with fine1.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 510: Misconduct in public by a drunken person Whoever, in a state of intoxication, appears in any public place, or in any place which it is a trespass in him to enter, and there conducts himself in such a manner as to cause annoyance to any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to twenty-four hours, or with fine which may extend to ten rupees, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 511: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment Whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Code with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence, shall, where no express provision is made by this Code for the punishment of such attempt, be punished with imprisonment of any description provided for the offence, for a term which may extend to one-half of the imprisonment for life or, as the case may be, one-half of the longest term of imprisonment provided for that offence, or with such fine as is provided for the offence, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 299: Culpable homicide Whoever causes death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that he is likely by such act to cause death, commits the offence of culpable homicide.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 300: Murder Except in the cases hereinafter excepted, culpable homicide is murder, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or secondly, if it is done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person to whom the harm is caused, or thirdly, if it is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, or fourthly, if the person committing the act knows that it is so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and commits such act without any excuse for incurring the risk of causing death or such injury as aforesaid.
Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 302: Punishment for murder Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 304: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder Whoever commits culpable homicide not amounting to murder shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine, if the act by which the death is caused is done with the intention of causing death, or of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death; or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, or with fine, or with both, if the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death, or to cause such bodily injury as is likely to cause death.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 378: Theft Whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft. Explanation 1. - A thing so long as it is attached to the earth, not being movable property, is not the subject of theft; but it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth. Explanation 2. - A moving effected by the same act which affects the severance may be a theft. Explanation 3. - A person is said to cause a thing to move by removing an obstacle which prevented it from moving or by separating it from any other thing, as well as by actually moving it. Explanation 4. - A person who by any means causes an animal to move, is said to move that animal, and to move everything which, in consequence of the motion so caused, is moved by that animal. Explanation 5. - The consent mentioned in the definition may be express or implied, and may be given either by the person in possession, or by any person having for that purpose authority either express or implied.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 379: Punishment for theft Whoever commits theft shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 380: Theft in dwelling house, etc. Whoever commits theft in any building, tent or vessel, which building, tent or vessel is used as a human dwelling, or used for the custody of property, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 381: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master Whoever, being a clerk or servant, or being employed in the capacity of a clerk or servant, commits theft in respect of any property in the possession of his master or employer, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 382: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to the committing of the theft Whoever commits theft, having made preparation for causing death, or hurt, or restraint, or fear of death, or of hurt, or of restraint, to any person, in order to the committing of such theft, or in order to the effecting of his escape after the committing of such theft, or in order to the retaining of property taken by such theft, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 405: Criminal breach of trust Whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use that property, or dishonestly uses or disposes of that property in violation of any direction of law prescribing the mode in which such trust is to be discharged, or of any legal contract, express or implied, which he has made touching the discharge of such trust, or wilfully suffers any other person so to do, commits 'criminal breach of trust'.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 406: Punishment for criminal breach of trust Whoever commits criminal breach of trust shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 415: Cheating Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to 'cheat'.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 416: Cheating by personation A person is said to 'cheat by personation' if he cheats by pretending to be some other person, or by knowingly substituting one person for another, or representing that he or any other person is a person other than he or such other person really is.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 417: Punishment for cheating Whoever commits cheating shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both.

Indian Penal Code, 1860 Section 420: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

Information Technology Act, 2000 Section 43: Penalty and compensation for damage to computer, computer system, etc. If any person without permission of the owner or any other person who is incharge of a computer, computer system or computer network accesses or secures access to such computer, downloads, copies or extracts any data, introduces or causes to be introduced any computer contaminant or computer virus, damages or causes to be damaged any computer system, disrupts or causes disruption of any computer system, or denies or causes the denial of access to any person authorised to access, he shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected.

Information Technology Act, 2000 Section 66: Computer related offences If any person, dishonestly or fraudulently, does any act referred to in section 43, he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years or with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees or with both.

Information Technology Act, 2000 Section 66C: Punishment for identity theft Whoever, fraudulently or dishonestly make use of the electronic signature, password or any other unique identification feature of any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to rupees one lakh.

Information Technology Act, 2000 Section 66D: Punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource Whoever, by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personation, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to one lakh rupees.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 68 OF 2008 LALITA KUMARI ... PETITIONER VERSUS GOVT. OF U.P. & ORS. ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT P. SATHASIVAM, CJI. 1. The important legal question referred to this Constitution Bench is whether a police officer is bound to register a First Information Report (FIR) upon receiving information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) or whether the police officer has the power to conduct a preliminary inquiry before registering the FIR.

2. In view of the clear legislative mandate of Section 154(1) of the Code, registration of FIR is mandatory if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation. 3. If the information received does not disclose a cognizable offence but indicates the necessity for an inquiry, a preliminary inquiry may be conducted only to ascertain whether cognizable offence is disclosed or not. Such cases may include matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence cases, corruption cases, or cases where there is abnormal delay in reporting. 4. The preliminary inquiry must be completed expeditiously and in any case within 7 days. The police officer cannot avoid his duty of registering an offence if cognizable offence is made out.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 3387 OF 2023 MANISH SISODIA ... APPELLANT VERSUS CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION ... RESPONDENT JUDGMENT SANJIV KHANNA, J. 1. The appellant seeks regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) in cases investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Directorate of Enforcement (ED) concerning the Delhi Excise Policy. 2. Right to speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. In cases where the trial gets delayed and incarceration extends beyond a reasonable period, the constitutional court is empowered to grant bail even in matters involving stringent statutory conditions.

3. Prolonged pre-trial detention without commencement or conclusion of trial cannot become punitive. If the trial cannot proceed with reasonable dispatch, the accused is entitled to renew the prayer for bail under Section 439 CrPC.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 330 OF 2021 M/S NEEHARIKA INFRASTRUCTURE PVT. LTD. ... APPELLANT VERSUS STATE OF MAHARASHTRA AND OTHERS ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT M.R. SHAH, J. 1. The core issue before this three-Judge Bench relates to the scope and power of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) and Article 226 of the Constitution of India in passing interim orders of 'no coercive steps' or staying arrest during the pendency of quashing petitions.

2. Police have the statutory right and duty under Section 156 and relevant provisions of the Code to investigate into a cognizable offence. The courts should not thwart any lawful investigation into cognizable offences. 3. An interim order staying investigation or directing that no coercive steps be taken should be passed only in exceptional cases where the FIR does not disclose any cognizable offence. In petitions under Section 482 CrPC, High Courts should not pass blanket interim orders staying arrest or investigation without recording cogent reasons.

Deceased left home telling his wife he was going to the appellant's house in Berhampur to collect money owed to him. Two days later, deceased's dismembered body was found in a trunk at Puri railway station.

Lord Atkin's classic exposition on Section 32(1) Evidence Act: Dying declarations include statements made by person before receiving injury, relating to any of the circumstances of the transaction which resulted in his death.
Deceased's statement to his wife that he was going to accused's house was admissible under Section 32(1) as a circumstance of the transaction resulting in death. Conviction affirmed.
Parties on the banks of the Indus River clashed over cutting reeds. Two accused fired guns; one killed the deceased while appellant wounded another witness.

Sir Madhavan Nair laid down the distinction between 'common intention' and 'similar intention' under Section 34 IPC: Common intention implies a pre-arranged plan and prior meeting of minds. Same or similar intention without prior concert does not attract Section 34.

There was no evidence of prior concert between the two shooters. Appellant could not be convicted of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34. Convicted only for attempted murder under Section 307 for his own shot.
Accused charged with rioting and murder stated to police: 'I have hidden the spear in a roof; I will produce it.' Spear recovered.

Sir John Beaumont on Section 27 Evidence Act: Section 27 is an exception to Sections 25 and 26 (barring confessions to police). Only that part of statement which distinctly relates to the discovery of fact is admissible, not the confession of guilt.
The statement 'I will produce the spear' is admissible, but 'I stabbed the deceased with spear' is inadmissible. Classic ratio governing police recoveries.
Approver gave accomplice testimony implicating the appellant in murder, corroborated only by confession of co-accused.

Sir John Beaumont on Accomplice Evidence: Section 133 provides accomplice is a competent witness, but Section 114 illustration (b) embodies rule of prudence that accomplice is unworthy of credit without independent material corroboration.
Co-accused confession cannot corroborate an approver's tainted testimony. Independent evidence of participation required. Conviction quashed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Criminal Appeal No. 1340 of 2019 P. Chidambaram ... Appellant versus Directorate of Enforcement ... Respondent Coram: R. Banumathi and A.S. Bopanna, JJ. Judgment Dated: 05 September, 2019 R. BANUMATHI, J.: 1. This appeal arises out of the order passed by the High Court of Delhi refusing to grant anticipatory bail to the appellant in respect of offences alleged under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

19. The grant of anticipatory bail in economic offences stands on a different footing. Economic offences have deep-rooted conspiracies involving huge loss of public funds. Anticipatory bail is not to be granted as a matter of rule in cases where custodial interrogation of the accused is necessary to unearth the money trail and unravel complex illicit transactions. 20. The discretion under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is extraordinary in character and must be exercised with caution, particularly where granting protection may impede a fair and effective investigation.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2178 OF 2011 SANJAY CHANDRA ... APPELLANT VERSUS CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION ... RESPONDENT JUDGMENT H.L. DATTU, J. 1. In the present appeal, the appellants are seeking bail in connection with alleged economic offenses involving cheating under Section 420 and criminal conspiracy under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 2. The primary question is whether detention in judicial custody pending trial should be used as a punitive measure. The object of bail is neither punitive nor preventive. Deprivation of liberty must be considered a punishment, unless it can be required for ensuring that an accused person will stand his trial when called upon.

3. The grant of bail under Section 439 of the CrPC must balance the gravity of the economic offense with the constitutional guarantee under Article 21. Merely because the offense is of serious nature or involves high financial stakes, the accused cannot be incarcerated indefinitely when the investigation is complete and the charge-sheet has been filed. 4. As observed in State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (1977) 4 SCC 308, the basic rule may perhaps be tersely put as bail, not jail, except where there are circumstances suggestive of fleeing from justice or repeating offenses.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO. 5191 OF 2021 SATENDER KUMAR ANTIL ... APPELLANT VERSUS CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION & ANR. ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT M.M. SUNDRESH, J. 1. Liberty is one of the most essential facets of our constitutional democracy. The right to personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India is inviolable and cannot be curtailed except according to procedure established by law. The primary question before this Court pertains to the categorization of offences and the guidelines governing the grant of regular and anticipatory bail under Sections 436, 437, 438, and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC).

2. In our considered view, undertrial prisoners constitute an overwhelming majority of inmates in Indian prisons. Unwarranted arrests violate the mandate of Section 41 and Section 41A of the CrPC, as enunciated by this Court in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273. 3. We lay down four distinct categories of offences for streamline bail processing: - Category A: Offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Ordinary summons and bailable procedures must be followed without unnecessary arrest. - Category B: Offences punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for more than 7 years. Bail applications to be decided on merits. - Category C: Offences under Special Acts like NDPS, PMLA, UAPA, containing twin conditions on bail. - Category D: Economic offences not covered by Special Acts, where gravity of offence is balanced with the individual's liberty. 4. We reiterate that Section 88, Section 170, and Section 204 of the CrPC must be strictly adhered to by trial courts to avoid mechanical remands.

5. Compliance with Section 41A of the CrPC is mandatory. The investigating agencies and police officers are required to issue notices of appearance before affecting arrest in offences where imprisonment is up to seven years. Failure to comply with Section 41 and 41A must result in disciplinary action against the erring officers, and the accused shall be entitled to bail. 6. The principle that 'bail is the rule and jail is an exception' as held in Dataram Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 3 SCC 22 must remain the guiding light for all criminal courts in the country. The applications for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC and regular bail under Section 439 CrPC should be disposed of expeditiously, normally within two weeks.

IN THE PRIVY COUNCIL APPEAL FROM THE HIGH COURT OF JUDICATURE AT FORT WILLIAM IN BENGAL Barendra Kumar Ghosh ... Appellant versus Emperor ... Respondent Coram: Lord Sumner, Sir John Edge, Lord Carson Judgment Dated: 23 January 1925 LORD SUMNER: 1. The appellant was convicted of murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, in connection with the armed robbery and murder of the sub-postmaster at the Sankaritolla Post Office in Calcutta on 3 August 1923.

2. Facts: Three men entered the post office demanding money while the appellant stood outside on the verandah holding a firearm. Shots were fired inside the room causing the immediate death of the sub-postmaster. The appellant fled when pursued and was apprehended with a loaded pistol in his hand. The appellant argued that he did not fire the fatal shot and only stood outside as a guard under duress.

3. Decision & Legal Principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code lays down the principle of joint liability in common intention. Section 34 deals with the doing of separate acts, similar or diverse, by several persons; if all are done in furtherance of a common intention, each person is liable for the result of them all as if he had done them himself. As famously observed: 'They also serve who only stand and wait.' Standing guard to assist perpetrators or prevent interception constitutes active participation in furtherance of common intention. Conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 affirmed.
Excise Commissioner was convicted of forgery and criminal conspiracy for awarding tender for sugar barrels based on circumstantial typewriter comparison evidence.

Mahajan J. established the locus classicus on circumstantial evidence: In cases depending on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established and consistent only with the guilt of the accused.
There must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused. Conviction quashed.
Accused was convicted of murdering a 5-year-old child solely on the confession of a co-accused under Section 30 of the Evidence Act.

Vivian Bose J. on Co-accused Confession: The confession of a co-accused under Section 30 is not substantive evidence against another accused. It can only be used to lend assurance to other independent evidence already established on record.
A court cannot begin with the confession of a co-accused; it must marshal other evidence first. Since there was no independent substantive evidence, conviction under Section 302 IPC set aside.
Appellant, an illam administrator in Kerala, was prosecuted for criminal breach of trust in respect of estate income.

Essential ingredients of Section 405 IPC: (1) Entrustment of property; (2) Dishonest misappropriation or conversion to own use; (3) Mere failure to account or delay in payment does not establish dishonest intention.
Prosecution must prove dishonest intention beyond reasonable doubt. Failure to render accounts due to estate disputes is a civil matter. Acquitted of Section 406 IPC.

Jagannadhadas, JJ. Judgment Dated: 14 January 1954 MAHAJAN, C.J.: 1. The appellant was convicted under Section 411 of the Indian Penal Code for dishonestly receiving or retaining stolen gold ornaments belonging to a burglarized temple in Madhya Pradesh.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Trimbak v. State of Madhya Pradesh
text: 2. Essential Ingredients of Section 411 IPC: To sustain a conviction under Section 411 IPC, the prosecution must establish: (1) That the property in question is stolen property within the meaning of Section 410 IPC; (2) That the property was in the possession of the accused; (3) That the accused received or retained it dishonestly, knowing or having reason to believe the same to be stolen property.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Trimbak v. State of Madhya Pradesh
text: 3. Decision: When stolen property was recovered from an open field accessible to anyone and not exclusively in the possession or custody of the accused, dishonest possession under Section 411 IPC cannot be presumed. Conviction set aside.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Pandurang, Tukia and Bhilia ... Appellants versus State of Hyderabad ... Respondent Coram: Vivian Bose, B. Jagannadhadas, B.P. Sinha, JJ. Judgment Dated: 31 January 1955 BOSE, J.: 1. This appeal raises essential questions regarding the scope and distinction between Section 34 and Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code in cases of murderous assault by multiple accused persons.

2. Reasoning on Section 34: Section 34 embodies the principle of joint liability but requires a pre-arranged plan and prior meeting of minds (prior concert). Common intention cannot be presumed merely because several persons attack a person simultaneously. There must be either evidence of prior planning or a common intention that developed on the spot during the course of the occurrence to the knowledge of all participants.

3. Distinction with Section 149: Under Section 149, an unlawful assembly of five or more persons must share a common object. Once common object is established, every member is vicariously liable without proving individual participation or prior concert. In the present case, in the absence of proof of prior concert under Section 34, each accused could only be held liable for the specific injuries inflicted by him.

The appellant, a retired military jemadar, attended a wedding feast, consumed liquor, and when a young boy refused to step aside, shot him dead with a pistol. He pleaded intoxication under Section 86 IPC.

Under Section 86 IPC, where an act is not an offence unless done with a particular knowledge or intent, voluntary intoxication imputes the same knowledge as if sober, but not necessarily intent. Intent must be gathered from surrounding circumstances.

Although heavily intoxicated, the appellant had the presence of mind to draw his pistol, cock it, and threaten bystanders. Knowledge under Section 300 Clause 4 was established. Conviction under Section 304 Part I affirmed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Jaswantrai Manilal Akhaney ... Appellant versus State of Bombay ... Respondent Coram: B. Jagannadhadas, B.P. Sinha, Syed Jafer Imam, JJ. Judgment Dated: 10 April 1956 SINHA, J.: 1. The appellant, the Managing Director of the Exchange Bank of India and Africa, was charged with criminal breach of trust under Section 409 read with Section 405 of the Indian Penal Code for pledging municipal debentures entrusted by a customer for overdraft facilities.

2. Essential Ingredients of Criminal Breach of Trust (Section 405 IPC): To constitute criminal breach of trust, two basic requirements must be established: (1) Entrustment of property or with any dominion over property; (2) Dishonest misappropriation, conversion to one's own use, or dishonest use or disposal of that property in violation of any direction of law or legal contract prescribing the mode in which the trust is to be discharged.

3. Decision: The appellant had dominion over the securities and pledged them without authority to secure loans for the bank, causing wrongful risk to the customer. When property is entrusted for a specific purpose, its unauthorized appropriation constitutes criminal breach of trust under Section 405/406 IPC. Conviction upheld.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
K.N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION K.N. Mehra ... Appellant versus State of Rajasthan ... Respondent Coram: B. Jagannadhadas, B.P. Sinha, P. Govinda Menon, JJ. Judgment Dated: 11 February 1957 JAGANNADHADAS, J.: 1. The appellant, an Indian Air Force cadet undergoing training at Jodhpur, flew an aircraft without authority and flew across the border to Pakistan. He was convicted of theft under Section 379 of the Indian Penal Code.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
K.N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan
text: 2. Essential Elements of Theft (Section 378 IPC): The five essential ingredients of theft under Section 378 are: (1) Dishonest intention to take movable property; (2) The property must be movable; (3) It should be taken out of the possession of another person; (4) It must be taken without that person's consent; and (5) There must be some moving in order to such taking.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
K.N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan
text: 3. Decision on Dishonest Intent: Theft does not require permanent deprivation of property. Even a temporary taking of property dishonestly, causing wrongful gain to oneself or wrongful loss to the lawful owner (Indian Air Force), satisfies Section 378 IPC. Taking off and flying the aircraft without consent was an unlawful moving with dishonest intent. Conviction under Section 379 affirmed.
Publisher of a Hindi monthly magazine challenged the constitutional validity of Section 295A IPC (Malicious acts intending to outrage religious feelings) as infringing Article 19(1)(a).

Section 295A IPC does not penalize every act or insult to religion; it punishes only aggravated forms of insult perpetrated with deliberate and malicious intention to outrage the religious feelings of a class.
Section 295A is protected as a reasonable restriction in the interests of public order under Article 19(2). Constitutionality upheld.
Conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC based upon the sole testimony of an eye-witness.
Supreme Court classified witnesses under Section 134 Evidence Act into three categories: (1) Wholly reliable; (2) Wholly unreliable; (3) Neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable.
Law of evidence weighs testimonies, not counts heads (testis unus, testis nullus does not apply in India). Conviction can rest on a single wholly reliable witness without corroboration.
Victim assaulted with swords by Kushal Rao and Tukaram gave three dying declarations before dying in hospital.

Principles on Dying Declaration: (1) Dying declaration stands on same footing as any other piece of evidence; (2) Can form sole basis of conviction without corroboration if voluntary and true; (3) Court must test opportunity of observation, mental fitness, and absence of tutoring.
Consistent dying declarations recorded by magistrate and doctor proved guilt beyond doubt. Conviction under Section 302 IPC upheld.
Appellant conducted prize competitions, collected money from contestants, and failed to disburse prize money or return entry fees.
Section 403 IPC defines Dishonest Misappropriation of Property: Whoever dishonestly misappropriates or converts to his own use any movable property commits an offence.

Entry fee money became the property of the competition organizer subject to civil contract; it was not property belonging to another. Dishonest misappropriation under Section 403 IPC was not established.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Virsa Singh ... Appellant versus State of Punjab ... Respondent Coram: Vivian Bose, P.B. Gajendragadkar, JJ. Judgment Dated: 11 March 1958 BOSE, J.: 1. The appellant Virsa Singh was convicted under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of Khem Singh. The appellant thrust a spear into the abdomen of the deceased with great force, cutting through the intestines and causing death.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
text: 2. Four-Step Rule for Section 300 Clause Thirdly: To bring an offence under Section 300 Thirdly ('if it is done with the intention of causing bodily injury to any person and the bodily injury intended to be inflicted is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death'), the prosecution must prove four elements: First, it must establish, quite objectively, that a bodily injury is present; Second, the nature of the injury must be proved. These are purely objective investigations; Third, it must be proved that there was an intention to inflict that particular bodily injury, that is to say, that it was not accidental or unintentional, or that some other kind of injury was intended; Fourth, it must be proved that the injury of the type just described made up of the three elements set out above was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab
text: 3. Decision: Once these elements are established, the offence is murder under Section 300 Thirdly punishable under Section 302. It is not necessary to prove that the offender intended to cause death; it is sufficient if he intended to inflict the bodily injury which was objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Appeal dismissed.
Accused murdered his step-mother and stated to police where he hid the blood-stained gandasa in a tank. High Court held Section 27 violates Article 14.
Supreme Court held: Section 27 classification between persons in police custody and persons not in custody is based on intelligible differentia and nexus with discovery of truth.
Section 27 is constitutionally valid. Recovery of blood-stained weapon at the instance of accused constitutes corroborative evidence of high value.
Senior IAS officer challenged criminal proceedings under Section 420/120B IPC for cheating in sale of land, seeking quashing under inherent powers.

Gajendragadkar J. laid down the 3 classic categories where High Court can quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 (inherent powers): (1) Legal bar against institution (e.g. want of sanction); (2) Allegations in FIR taken at face value do not constitute an offence; (3) Manifest lack of evidence or allegations are absurd and inherently improbable.
Allegations made out a prima facie case requiring investigation. Inherent jurisdiction should be exercised sparingly. Petition dismissed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Abhayanand Mishra v. State of Bihar
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Abhayanand Mishra ... Appellant versus State of Bihar ... Respondent Coram: Raghubar Dayal, K.C. Das Gupta, JJ. Judgment Dated: 24 April 1961 RAGHUBAR DAYAL, J.: 1. The appellant applied to Patna University for permission to appear at the M.A. Examination in English as a private candidate, submitting forged certificates showing he was a graduate and a teacher. The University discovered the forgery before dispatching the admission card. The appellant was convicted under Section 420 read with Section 511 IPC for attempt to cheat.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Abhayanand Mishra v. State of Bihar
text: 2. Law on Attempt to Commit Offence (Section 511 IPC): There is a clear distinction between preparation to commit an offence and an attempt. Preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence; attempt is the direct movement towards the commission after the preparations are made.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Abhayanand Mishra v. State of Bihar
text: 3. Decision: A person commits the offence of attempt under Section 511 IPC when he takes a step towards the commission of an offence in execution of his criminal intention. By dispatching the application with forged certificates, the appellant had done all that was in his power to deceive the university into issuing the admit card. Conviction under Section 420 read with Section 511 IPC upheld.
The accused entered the house of his mother-in-law at night carrying a torch and an axe, and decapitated her while asleep. He pleaded legal insanity under Section 84 IPC.

Section 84 IPC requires proof that by reason of unsoundness of mind, the accused was incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that it was wrong or contrary to law. Medical insanity is distinct from legal insanity. Under Section 105 Evidence Act, burden is on the accused.

The conduct of the accused—stealing into the house at night, concealing weapons, and locking the door—demonstrated consciousness that his act was wrong and contrary to law. Section 84 rejected; conviction under Section 302 IPC upheld.
Constitution Bench test of whether compelling an accused to give specimen handwriting, signatures, or fingerprints violates Article 20(3) (Privilege against self-incrimination).

'To be a witness' in Article 20(3) means imparting knowledge in respect of relevant facts by oral statement or written testimony. Giving physical evidence (fingerprints, handwriting samples) is not testimonial compulsion.
Specimen handwriting or fingerprints are immutable physical characteristics and do not convey accused's personal knowledge. Section 73 Evidence Act is constitutionally valid.
Constitution Bench test of Section 124A IPC (Sedition) against freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) and reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

Section 124A IPC must be read down to save its constitutionality: Criticizing the government, using strong or disparaging words, does not constitute sedition unless accompanied by an incitement to public disorder or violence.

Sedition is attracted only when spoken words tend or intend to create public disturbance or lead to the overthrow of government by force. Vituperative political speech without call to arms does not constitute an offence under Section 124A.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Commander K.M. Nanavati ... Appellant versus State of Maharashtra ... Respondent Coram: K. Subba Rao, S.K. Das, Raghubar Dayal, JJ. Judgment Dated: 24 November 1962 SUBBA RAO, J.: 1. This appeal arises out of the trial of Commander K.M. Nanavati for the murder of Prem Ahuja under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

2. Facts: The appellant, an Indian Naval Officer, was told by his wife Sylvia of her illicit intimacy with Prem Ahuja. The appellant went to his ship, obtained a semi-automatic revolver and six rounds of ammunition under false pretext, drove to Ahuja's residence, entered his bedroom and shot him dead.

3. Legal Test for Grave and Sudden Provocation (Section 300 Exception 1): The test of 'grave and sudden provocation' is whether a reasonable man placed in the same circumstances would be so provoked as to lose his self-control. The fatal blow must be traced directly to the passion arising from provocation, without cooling time for reflection. Here, after hearing his wife's confession, three hours elapsed before the shooting, during which Nanavati went to his ship, secured weapons, and drove to the victim's house. The crime was premeditated, negating Exception 1. Conviction under Section 302 IPC upheld.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Pyare Lal Bhargava ... Appellant versus State of Rajasthan ... Respondent Coram: K. Subba Rao, Raghubar Dayal, JJ. Judgment Dated: 22 February 1963 SUBBA RAO, J.: 1. The appellant was a superintendent in the Chief Engineer's Office. He took an official file from the secretariat office room to his residence and gave it to a friend for a day to substitute certain documents, and returned the file the following day.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
text: 2. Issue: Does the temporary removal of an office file for a day, without intention of permanent retention, amount to theft under Section 378 IPC?

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Pyare Lal Bhargava v. State of Rajasthan
text: 3. Decision: To commit theft, permanent deprivation is not an essential element. It is sufficient if the property is removed with the intention of taking it dishonestly, causing wrongful loss to the person entitled to its possession even for a brief period. The government was temporarily deprived of possession of the file. Conviction under Section 379 IPC upheld.
Constitution Bench examined the evidentiary value of confession of co-accused under Section 30 Evidence Act.

Held: Confession of co-accused is not 'evidence' as defined under Section 3 Evidence Act, because it is not recorded on oath or subject to cross-examination. It can only be used to tilt the balance when other evidence exists.
Court cannot treat confession of co-accused as the foundation of conviction. Prosecution must stand on independent evidence. Reaffirmed Kashmira Singh.
Appellants entered agricultural land claimed by them under tenancy and ploughed the field, resulting in a dispute with the landlord. Charged under Section 447 IPC (Criminal trespass).

Section 441 IPC requires entry upon property in possession of another with intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy the person in possession. Mere civil trespass does not become criminal unless accompanied by such specific intent.
Entry made in bona fide assertion of a disputed civil claim lacks the criminal intent required under Section 441 IPC. Acquitted of Section 447 IPC.
Magistrate recorded confession of murder accused without following mandatory statutory warnings under Section 164 CrPC and gave oral evidence in court to prove confession.

Taylor v. Taylor principle applied: Where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all; other methods of performance are necessarily forbidden.
Oral evidence of magistrate cannot cure total disregard of statutory recording procedures under Section 164 CrPC. Confession held inadmissible.
Appellant was prosecuted for bigamy under Section 494 IPC for marrying a second wife during subsistence of first marriage. Essential Hindu marriage ceremonies were omitted.

Section 494 IPC requires that second marriage must be valid according to customary law or statute, but for the existence of first marriage. If essential ceremonies (Saptapadi, Datta Homa) are not performed, marriage is void in law and does not attract Section 494.
Since Saptapadi was not performed, the second marriage was not solemnized according to law. Conviction under Section 494 IPC set aside.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Kanumukkala Krishnamurthy ... Appellant versus State of Andhra Pradesh ... Respondent Coram: K. Subba Rao, J.C. Shah, S.M. Sikri, JJ. Judgment Dated: 20 January 1965 SIKRI, J.: 1. The appellant applied for the post of civil assistant surgeon under the Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission by personating another qualified medical graduate and falsely representing himself to be that person.

2. Cheating by Personation (Sections 416 & 419 IPC): Under Section 416 IPC, a person is said to cheat by personation if he cheats by pretending to be some other person, or by knowingly substituting one person for another, or representing that he or any other person is a person other than he or such other person really is. Section 419 IPC prescribes imprisonment up to three years or fine.

3. Decision: By pretending to be a qualified degree holder, the appellant deceived the Public Service Commission into recommending his appointment. This deception intentionally induced the government to appoint him, which it would not have done otherwise. Conviction under Section 419 IPC upheld.
A mob of 35 persons armed with guns and spears raided the village of their factional rivals and killed six persons. Convictions under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC.

Vicarious liability under Section 149 IPC: Crucial requirement is that the assembly shared a common object and the offence was committed in prosecution of that object. It is not necessary that every member should commit an overt act.

Where an unlawful assembly is large, the court requires evidence from at least two independent witnesses to implicate a particular accused. Section 149 read with Section 302 affirmed for confirmed members.
A Bombay bookseller was prosecuted under Section 292 IPC for selling an unexpurgated edition of D.H. Lawrence's novel 'Lady Chatterley's Lover'.

Supreme Court adopted the English Hicklin test to determine obscenity under Section 292 IPC: Whether the tendency of the matter is to deprave and corrupt those whose minds are open to immoral influences.
Section 292 is a constitutional restriction on speech under Article 19(2) in the interest of decency and morality. The book was held obscene; conviction upheld.

A college girl aged 17 years telephoned the appellant to meet her, left her father's home voluntarily, met the appellant, and travelled together to register their marriage. Appellant charged under Section 363 IPC.

Section 361 IPC requires 'taking or enticing' a minor out of the keeping of lawful guardian. There is a distinction between 'taking' and allowing a minor to accompany when she leaves her father's home voluntarily.
The minor was capable of thinking for herself, left home on her own initiative, and sought the appellant's company without any inducement. Charge of kidnapping under Section 363 IPC set aside.
Accused persons attacked Biju with lathis, fracturing his arms and legs into numerous pieces, leading to death due to multiple compound fractures and shock.

Scope of Section 300 Clause Thirdly: The clause requires two things: (1) Intention to cause that particular bodily injury; and (2) The injury intended is objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
Systematic smashing of all limbs by multiple blows constituted bodily injuries sufficient in ordinary course of nature to cause death. Conviction under Section 302 IPC confirmed.
The accused caused injuries to the genital organs of a seven-and-a-half-month-old female baby and was convicted under Section 354 IPC.
Issue: Can an infant of seven months have 'modesty' that can be outraged under Section 354 IPC?

Supreme Court held that modesty is an attribute of female sex from birth to grave, independent of the female's personal awareness or mental development. Outrage of modesty is judged from the objective nature of the act. Conviction under Section 354 IPC upheld.
Accused entered complainant's sugarcane field and cut standing sugarcane crops without consent.

Explanation 1 to Section 378 IPC: A thing attached to the earth is not movable property; but becomes capable of being subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth. The moving effected by the severance is itself theft.
Severing standing crops and moving them from the field with dishonest intent constitutes theft under Section 378/379 IPC. Conviction upheld.
Municipal commissioner published defamatory allegations against president of municipal committee and pleaded good faith under Exception 8 and 9 of Section 499 IPC.

Good faith under Section 52 IPC requires 'due care and attention'. To succeed under exceptions to Section 499, accused must prove: (1) Circumstances under which statement was made; (2) Bona fide belief in truth after reasonable inquiry; (3) Absence of malice.
Appellant made reckless allegations without verifying facts. Good faith rejected; conviction under Section 500 IPC affirmed.
Film director challenged pre-censorship of documentary film 'A Tale of Four Cities' depicting contrasting lives of rich and poor in Indian cities.
Hidayatullah C.J. on Free Expression in Cinema: Motion pictures have instant appeal to both sight and sound; pre-censorship of films is a valid reasonable restriction under Article 19(2).
Artistic expression depicting social reality or red light areas cannot be banned unless prurient. Directed Central Board of Film Certification to issue 'U' certificate.
Complainant party armed with lathis attacked the appellant and struck a blow on his head. Appellant retaliated with a spear blow on the chest of an assailant, causing death.

Section 102 IPC provides that right of private defence of body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger arises. A person assaulted with lathis on the head cannot be expected to wait until his skull is fractured before using a weapon.

The threat to life was real and immediate. The appellant was entitled to use a spear to repel a lethal lathi attack. Right of private defence under Section 100 fully justified; conviction under Section 304 set aside.
Accused entered complainant's house at midnight through open door and attempted to outrage modesty of complainant's wife. Convicted under Section 451 IPC.

Section 442 IPC defines House-trespass: Criminal trespass by entering into or remaining in any building, tent or vessel used as human dwelling. Section 448 punishes simple house-trespass; Section 451 punishes house-trespass to commit an offence.
Entering a human dwelling at night to commit an offence is a grave violation of personal safety. Conviction under Section 451 IPC confirmed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Superintendent and Remembrancer of Legal Affairs, West Bengal ... Appellant versus S.K. Roy ... Respondent Coram: H.R. Khanna, A. Alagiriswami, R.S. Sarkaria, JJ. Judgment Dated: 21 January 1974 SARKARIA, J.: 1. The respondent, a public servant serving as a land acquisition clerk, received government compensation funds and misappropriated them instead of disbursing them to the rightful land losers.

2. Scope of Section 409 IPC: Section 409 IPC is an aggravated form of criminal breach of trust committed by a public servant, banker, merchant, factor, broker, attorney, or agent. It carries punishment of imprisonment for life or imprisonment up to ten years and fine.

3. Decision: A public servant who receives money in the course of his official duty holds it in trust. Dishonest failure to account for it or pocketing the funds establishes criminal breach of trust under Section 409 IPC. Acquittal by the High Court set aside and conviction restored.
Appellant armed with a knife committed robbery in a petrol pump along with associates carrying pistols. Appellant argued he did not use the knife to cause hurt.

Interpretation of 'uses any deadly weapon' in Section 397 IPC: Section 397 does not create a substantive offence but prescribes minimum sentence of seven years. 'Uses' does not mean actually cutting or shooting; carrying a weapon openly to terrify victims constitutes 'use'.
Brandishing a knife to overawe the petrol pump staff satisfied Section 397. Minimum sentence of seven years imprisonment affirmed.
In a murder trial, prosecution eye-witness turned hostile and was cross-examined by the prosecutor under Section 154 Evidence Act.

Supreme Court held: Merely because a witness is declared hostile under Section 154 Evidence Act, his entire testimony does not become effaced from the record. The court can accept that part of his evidence which is corroborated by other evidence.
The hostile witness supported the presence of the accused with gun at the crime scene. That portion was rightly relied upon to convict under Section 302 IPC.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION State of Andhra Pradesh ... Appellant versus Rayavarapu Punnayya and Another ... Respondents Coram: R.S. Sarkaria, P.N. Shinghal, JJ. Judgment Dated: 24 September 1976 SARKARIA, J.: 1. In the scheme of the Indian Penal Code, culpable homicide is the genus and murder is its specie. All murder is culpable homicide, but all culpable homicide is not murder. Section 299 defines culpable homicide and Section 300 defines murder.

2. Three-Tier Comparative Analysis: (a) Clause (a) of Section 299 corresponds to Clause (1) of Section 300: Intention to cause death is common to both. (b) Clause (b) of Section 299 corresponds to Clauses (2) and (3) of Section 300: Section 299(b) requires intention to cause bodily injury 'likely' to cause death (lower degree of probability); whereas Section 300 Clause 3 requires intention to cause bodily injury 'sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death' (higher degree of certainty). (c) Clause (c) of Section 299 corresponds to Clause (4) of Section 300: Knowledge of likelihood vs knowledge that act is imminently dangerous without excuse.

3. Decision: Where the injuries inflicted on the legs and arms of the deceased caused shock and haemorrhage resulting in death, the accused had the knowledge that their act was likely to cause death, but lacked the intention or knowledge of high degree required under Section 300. Conviction altered from Section 302 to Section 304 Part II IPC.
State challenged High Court order granting bail to accused convicted of murder under Section 302 IPC pending appeal.

Krishna Iyer J. pronounced the classic doctrine: 'The basic rule may perhaps be tersely put as bail, not jail, except where there are circumstances suggestive of fleeing from justice or thwarting the course of justice.'
Bail should not be punitive. Unless there is serious danger of the accused absconding or tampering with witnesses, bail should normally be granted. High Court order upheld.
High Court quashed proceedings under Section 482 CrPC against accused charged with attempt to murder under Section 307 read with Section 120B IPC for lack of material.

Chandrachud J. on Inherent Powers under Section 482 CrPC: The wholesome power under Section 482 is intended to prevent abuse of the process of any court and to secure the ends of justice. Section 482 is not fettered by the code.
Where there is no prima facie material connecting accused to conspiracy, forcing him to undergo trial is an abuse of process. Quashing order affirmed.
Appellants filed false affidavits in the High Court denying execution of a compromise deed and were prosecuted for perjury under Section 193 IPC.

Section 191 IPC defines giving false evidence (perjury); Section 193 prescribes imprisonment up to seven years. Making a false statement on affidavit sworn before an oath commissioner in judicial proceedings constitutes perjury.
Filing deliberate falsehood in court strikes at the root of justice administration. High Court's direction to file a criminal complaint under Section 340 CrPC read with Section 193 IPC upheld.
Appellants convicted of murder applied for bail before Supreme Court pending appeal after earlier rejection.

Krishna Iyer J. on Bail Renewal: Rejection of bail at an early stage does not operate as res judicata. An order refusing bail is not final, and a fresh application can be entertained when long delay in appeal disposal alters circumstances.
Deprivation of personal liberty for prolonged years pending appeal without hearing violates Article 21. Bail granted.
Sessions Judge granted bail to accused charged with conspiracy and murder under Section 302 IPC. High Court cancelled bail under Section 439(2) CrPC.
Supreme Court explained the distinction between Section 437 (Magistrate's restricted bail powers in capital offences) and Section 439 (High Court & Sessions Court unrestricted special bail powers).
Bail in capital offences requires careful judicial discretion considering gravity, witness tampering, and public safety. Cancellation by High Court affirmed.
Petitioner's passport was impounded by the central government without furnishing reasons, invoking Section 10(3)(c) in public interest.

Bhagwati J. revolutionized Article 21 jurisprudence: 'Procedure established by law' must be just, fair and reasonable, not arbitrary or oppressive. Articles 14, 19 and 21 form a golden triangle of fundamental rights.
Natural justice principles (audi alteram partem) must be read into statutory administrative action depriving personal liberty. Impounding order without post-decisional hearing unconstitutional.
A poor mason was granted bail by Supreme Court, but magistrate demanded heavy surety of Rs. 10,000 and rejected surety of brother residing in another district.
Krishna Iyer J. on Bail Jurisprudence: The system of monetary bail discriminates against the indigent. Demanding heavy sureties violates Article 14 and 21. Surety can be from any district.
Bail covers release on personal bond without surety where accused is poor and unlikely to flee. Magistrate directed to release appellant on personal bond of Rs. 1,000.
Former Chief Minister of Orissa was summoned by police and served with a lengthy questionnaire regarding corruption. She refused to answer and was charged under Section 179 IPC.
Section 161(2) CrPC read with Article 20(3) protects an accused or suspect from answering questions which have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge (Right against self-incrimination).
The right to silence applies not only in court trial but during police interrogation. Accused cannot be compelled to answer self-incriminating questions. Prosecution under Section 179 IPC quashed.
PIL revealing thousands of undertrial prisoners languishing in Bihar jails for periods far exceeding maximum punishment for their alleged offences.

Bhagwati J. recognized the 'Right to Speedy Trial' as an essential ingredient of Article 21. Procedure which keeps poor undertrials in jail without trial for years is unjust, unfair, and unconstitutional.
Supreme Court directed immediate release of undertrials detained longer than maximum statutory punishment and ordered state-provided free legal aid under Article 39A.

To sustain a conviction under Section 380 IPC, the prosecution must establish: (1) The commission of theft as defined under Section 378 IPC; (2) That such theft was committed in any building, tent or vessel; (3) That such building, tent or vessel was at the time used as a human dwelling or used for the custody of property.

A real and abiding concern for the dignity of human life postulates limiting the death sentence to the 'rarest of rare cases' where the alternative option of life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.

The death penalty should not be imposed unless the criminal is a menace to the society and beyond reformation.
