IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Criminal Appeal No. 335 of 1978 Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and Others ... Appellants versus State of Punjab ... Respondent Coram: Y.V. Chandrachud, C.J., P.N. Bhagwati, N.L. Untwalia, V.D. Tulzapurkar and A.P. Sen, JJ. Judgment Dated: 09 April, 1980 CHANDRACHUD, C.J. delivered the Judgment of the Constitution Bench: 1. The questions involved in this appeal turn on the true scope and meaning of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. That section confers on the High Court and the Court of Session the power to grant anticipatory bail to persons apprehending arrest in non-bailable offences.

14. We find ourselves unable to accept the contention that the power under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be exercised only in exceptional cases. The High Court has observed that the power is of an extraordinary character and must be sparingly used. No such limitation is contained in the section. The Legislature conferred this power to protect personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. 15. The right to personal liberty is too precious a value of our constitutional system to be subordinated to any consideration except the clear mandate of law. An arbitrary arrest causes irreparable harm to the reputation and self-esteem of a citizen.

35. In conclusion, the principles relating to the grant of anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC may be summarized as follows: (a) The power to grant anticipatory bail is not unguided; it must be exercised according to judicial discretion considering the nature and seriousness of the accusation, the antecedents of the applicant, and the possibility of fleeing from justice. (b) The operation of an order of anticipatory bail should not be mechanically limited to a specified duration or until the filing of the charge-sheet. (c) Anticipatory bail can be granted even after the filing of the FIR, or before the FIR is lodged, provided there is a reasonable apprehension of arrest on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence.
Customs officers intercepted truck near seashore at midnight carrying silver ingots, alongside a mechanized seafaring vessel waiting near the creek.

Section 511 IPC (Attempt): What constitutes an attempt as distinct from preparation? An attempt is committed when an overt act is done in execution of criminal intent, which would lead to commission of offence unless interrupted by outside agency.

Transporting silver to the lonely creek where sea vessel was waiting was an overt step towards export. Interruption by customs officers alone stopped the commission. Conviction under Section 511 affirmed.
Open drains and stench from liquor factory caused public nuisance to residents in Ratlam. Magistrate ordered municipality to construct drainage under Section 133 CrPC.

Public nuisance under Section 268 IPC: An act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public. Municipalities cannot plead lack of financial resources to escape mandatory statutory duty to abate nuisance.
Human rights and dignity under Article 21 require decent living conditions. Section 133 CrPC is a public duty weapon against municipal default. Order compelling construction of drainage affirmed.
The appellant, an industrialist travelling in a car, was stopped by unruly workers demanding bonus. Appellant fired three revolver shots into the ground and one into the crowd, killing a worker.

Section 100 IPC permits causing death in private defence only if the assault causes reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt. Force used must not exceed what is strictly necessary under Section 99 IPC.

The crowd was unarmed and only shouting slogans. There was no apprehension of death or grievous hurt to justify killing. Appellant exceeded the right of private defence under Exception 2 to Section 300. Conviction altered to Section 304 Part II IPC.
Police officers opened fire under orders of the Deputy Commissioner of Police during violent mob attacks in Calcutta, resulting in deaths. Accused claimed protection under Section 76 IPC.

Section 76 IPC protects a person who by reason of a mistake of fact and not of law in good faith believes himself to be bound by law to do the act. An order of a superior officer to fire on a riotous mob is a complete defence unless palpably illegal.
The firing was ordered by a competent superior officer to control an armed mob attacking police personnel. The subordinate police officers were bound by law to obey. Acquittal affirmed.
In a feud between families, Machhi Singh and 11 associates raided five villages at night and murdered 17 persons including women and sleeping children.

Supreme Court concretized Bachan Singh's 'Rarest of Rare' test into 5 specific categories: (1) Manner of murder (extreme brutality/torture); (2) Motive (contract killing/depravity); (3) Anti-social or socially abhorrent nature (bride burning); (4) Magnitude of crime (multiple murders); (5) Personality of victim (helpless child/woman).
Multiple murders of 17 innocent persons in midnight raid shocked the conscience of the community. Death sentence confirmed.
Manju died of potassium cyanide poisoning 4 months after marriage. Husband prosecuted based on circumstantial evidence.

Five Golden Principles (Panchsheel) of Circumstantial Evidence: (1) Circumstances must be fully established; (2) Facts must be consistent only with guilt; (3) Conclusive nature; (4) Must exclude every hypothesis of innocence; (5) Chain of evidence so complete as to leave no reasonable ground for conclusion consistent with innocence.
Possibility of suicide was not excluded; poison administration was not traced to husband. Prosecution failed to establish complete chain. Conviction under Section 302 set aside.
Accused murdered his wife and two infant children. Acquitted by High Court because of minor discrepancies in prosecution witness statements.
Supreme Court held: While appreciating evidence of witnesses, minor discrepancies or embellishments due to lapse of time or memory do not warrant rejection of credible testimony.

Court must look at broad human probability and core truth. Unrealistic standards of mathematical exactness should not be applied to rural witnesses. Acquittal reversed; conviction under Section 302 IPC restored.
Conspiracy to assassinate Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by security guards Beant Singh and Satwant Singh, with Kehar Singh as an conspirator under Section 120B IPC.

Section 120A IPC: The agreement is the crux of the offence. Direct evidence of conspiracy is seldom available. Section 10 Evidence Act allows statements and acts of co-conspirators in reference to common design as evidence against all.

Secret meetings between Beant Singh and Kehar Singh at the Golden Temple, religious instigation, and post-crime conduct proved criminal conspiracy under Section 120B read with Section 302 IPC. Death sentence confirmed.
Accused arrested in kidnapping case fell ill during initial 15-day remand. CBI sought police custody after expiry of the 15-day period.
Section 167(2) CrPC interpretation: Total period of police custody cannot exceed 15 days from the date of initial production before magistrate. Subsequent remand can only be judicial custody.
Even if the accused could not be interrogated during initial 15 days due to hospitalization, police custody cannot be granted after expiry of the first 15 days.
Constitution Bench formulated 11 comprehensive propositions governing the right to speedy trial under Article 21 in criminal prosecutions.

Held: Fair, just and reasonable procedure under Article 21 encompasses right to speedy trial. However, no outer time limit can be fixed for conclusion of criminal proceedings; delay must be balanced against systemic constraints and conduct of accused.
If systemic delay violates right to speedy trial, court can quash proceedings or reduce sentence depending on circumstances.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 729 OF 1990 STATE OF HARYANA AND OTHERS ... APPELLANTS VERSUS CH. BHAJAN LAL AND OTHERS ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT S. RATNAVEL PANDIAN, J. 1. This appeal raises vital questions regarding the scope and ambit of the inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) and the extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India to quash a First Information Report (FIR) and criminal proceedings.

2. In the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code, the following categories of cases are illustrated by way of guide where such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice: (1) Where the allegations made in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused. (2) Where the allegations in the FIR and other materials accompanying it do not disclose a cognizable offence justifying investigation by police officers under Section 156(1) of the Code. (3) Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the FIR or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused. (4) Where the allegations in the FIR do not constitute a cognizable offence but constitute only a non-cognizable offence, no investigation is permitted without an order of a Magistrate as contemplated under Section 155(2) of the Code. (5) Where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint are so absurd and inherently improbable that no prudent person can ever reach a just conclusion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding. (6) Where there is an express legal bar engrafted in any of the provisions of the Code or the concerned Act to the institution and continuance of the proceedings. (7) Where a criminal proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fide and/or where the proceeding is maliciously instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance.
Constitution Bench examined the 'indefeasible right' to default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC / Section 20(4) TADA upon expiry of statutory remand period.

The right to default bail accrues on expiry of 180/90 days and remains enforceable until the chargesheet is filed. If chargesheet is filed before the accused applies for default bail, the right is extinguished.
Accused must avail the right before filing of chargesheet by being ready to furnish bail. Principles governing statutory remand authoritatively settled.
Appellants raised slogans 'Khalistan Zindabad' outside a cinema hall in Chandigarh on the day Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated. They were charged under Sections 124A and 153A IPC.
Raising casual slogans a couple of times without an intention to incite violence or public disorder does not attract Section 124A (Sedition) or Section 153A (Promoting enmity between groups).
There was no reaction or public disturbance following the slogans. Over-sensitiveness to casual slogans would render free speech illusory. Conviction quashed.
Senior IAS officer Rupan Deol Bajaj filed an FIR alleging that Director General of Police K.P.S. Gill slapped her posterior at an official dinner party. High Court quashed the FIR.

Supreme Court defined 'modesty' under Section 354 IPC as the reserve of a woman that protects her sex. Any act which offends feminine decency or is suggestive of sex constitutes an outrage of modesty.
Slapping a woman's posterior in a social gathering was inherently indecent and outrage of modesty. High Court order set aside; prosecution under Section 354 and Section 509 IPC directed to proceed.
Hindu husband converted to Islam to marry a second wife without dissolving his first Hindu marriage, claiming Muslim personal law permits four wives.
Supreme Court held: A Hindu marriage solemnized under the Hindu Marriage Act can only be dissolved under that Act. Conversion to Islam does not dissolve the prior marriage.
Second marriage of a converted Hindu during lifetime of first wife is void and punishable as bigamy under Section 494 IPC. Emphasized need for Uniform Civil Code.
Constitution Bench test of Section 309 IPC (Attempt to commit suicide) and Section 306 IPC (Abetment of suicide) in light of Article 21 right to life.
Article 21 guarantees 'right to life' which includes right to live with dignity; it does not include the 'right to die'. Extinction of life is not a natural culmination of life.
Overruled P. Rathinam (1994). Section 306 and Section 309 IPC are constitutionally valid. Assisting or abetting someone to end life is an offence.
A 16-year-old girl was abducted in a car and gang-raped by three accused persons. Trial court acquitted accused doubting prosecutrix testimony for lack of corroboration.

Supreme Court held: The testimony of a victim of sexual assault stands on higher footing than an ordinary injured witness. Corroboration is not a rule of law, but of prudence. A prosecutrix cannot be treated as an accomplice.
Insistence on corroboration adds insult to injury. Trial courts must conduct trials of sexual offences in camera with sensitivity. Acquittal reversed; accused convicted under Section 376(2)(g) IPC.
PIL against custodial violence and torture by police. Supreme Court formulated 11 mandatory guidelines to be followed in all cases of arrest and detention.

Guidelines: (1) Arresting officer must wear visible badge; (2) Memo of arrest with witness signature; (3) Inform friend/relative within 8-12 hours; (4) Medical examination every 48 hours; (5) Right to meet lawyer during interrogation.
Custodial violence violates Article 21 and rule of law. Failure to follow guidelines makes police officers liable for departmental action and contempt of court.
Armed gang intercepted a taxi, threatened the driver with chopper, and took away cash and gold ornaments.

Section 390 IPC defines Robbery: In every robbery there is either theft or extortion. Theft becomes robbery if the offender, in order to the committing of theft, voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death, hurt, or wrongful restraint.
Threatening with chopper and tying up the driver caused wrongful restraint to effectuate theft. Offence fell squarely under Section 392 read with Section 397 IPC.
Wife filed complaint before magistrate alleging offences under Sections 498A and 406 IPC. Magistrate directed police to register FIR and investigate under Section 156(3) CrPC.
Supreme Court held: When a magistrate directs investigation under Section 156(3) CrPC, police are legally bound to register an FIR under Section 154 CrPC and conduct full statutory investigation.
Magistrate's order directing registration of FIR is within statutory jurisdiction. High Court order setting aside magistrate's direction quashed.
Newspaper published report of questions and answers in Maharashtra State Legislative Assembly regarding misappropriation of government funds by complainant.
Exception 4 to Section 499 IPC: It is not defamation to publish a substantially true report of the proceedings of a Court of Justice or of a Legislature.
The news item was an accurate report of what transpired on the floor of the Assembly, published without malice in public interest. Exception 4 attracted; complaint quashed.
Conspiracy to assassinate former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi by suicide bomber Dhanu at Sriperumbudur on 21 May 1991, orchestrated by the LTTE.

Principles of Section 120B IPC: An accused cannot be convicted of conspiracy unless it is established that he had knowledge of the object of conspiracy and agreed to participate in its execution. Mere association or rendering shelter without knowledge of the murder plot does not make one a conspirator.

Nalini accompanied the human bomber to the rally knowing the mission was to kill Rajiv Gandhi. Her active role in the conspiracy under Section 120B read with Section 302 IPC was proved beyond reasonable doubt.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma and Others ... Appellants versus State of Bihar and Another ... Respondents Coram: D.P. Wadhwa, S.S.M. Quadri, JJ. Judgment Dated: 31 March 2000 QUADRI, J.: 1. This appeal deals with the boundary between a civil breach of contract and criminal cheating under Section 415 and Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

2. Distinction Between Breach of Contract and Cheating: In breach of contract, the failure to perform may be due to subsequent contingencies or inability. In cheating, there must be a fraudulent or dishonest intention right at the beginning (inception) of the transaction. Mere inability of the promisor to deliver or honour a cheque at a later date does not constitute criminal cheating unless fraudulent intention existed ab initio.

3. Decision: In the absence of an allegation that the appellants had no intention to execute the sale deed or honour the contract at the inception, the dispute is purely civil. Criminal proceedings under Section 420 IPC quashed.
Review of Sarla Mudgal ruling on whether prosecuting a Hindu husband for bigamy under Section 494 IPC upon sham conversion to Islam infringes Article 25 religious freedom.
Held: Freedom of religion under Article 25 is subject to public order, morality, and health. Feigning religious conversion to commit bigamy is a fraud on personal law and religion.
Section 494 IPC applies equally to all persons whose first marriage subsists in law. Conviction under Section 494 does not violate Article 25. Review petition dismissed.
Accused entered prosecutrix's room, threatened her with dire consequences, and committed rape. Trial court held lack of physical struggle implied consent.
Consent vs Submission: Submission under fear of injury or intimidation is not free consent under Section 375 IPC. Absence of physical resistance or scratch marks does not prove consent.
Passive submission under threat cannot be equated with voluntary consent. Conviction under Section 376 IPC restored.
Appellant engaged in a quarrel with his sister's husband and told him to 'go and die'. Two days later, the husband committed suicide, naming the appellant in a suicide note.

Abetment under Section 107 read with Section 306 IPC requires active instigation or intentional aiding. Uttering words 'go and die' in the heat of a quarrel does not satisfy the mens rea of instigation.
Suicide was committed 48 hours after the quarrel; the deceased had ample time to reflect. Criminal proceedings under Section 306 IPC quashed.
Husband and wife settled matrimonial dispute mutually, agreed for divorce by mutual consent, and sought quashing of Section 498A IPC FIR under Section 482 CrPC.
Issue: Does the non-compoundable nature of Section 498A IPC under Section 320 CrPC limit the High Court's inherent power under Section 482 CrPC to quash proceedings upon compromise?
Supreme Court held: Section 320 CrPC does not limit Section 482. In matrimonial disputes where parties have genuinely settled, quashing FIR under Section 498A serves the ends of justice. FIR quashed.
A verbal quarrel erupted over cattle grazing, escalating suddenly into a clash where the accused struck the deceased on the head with a lathi, causing death. Pleaded Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC.

Four ingredients of Exception 4 to Section 300 (Sudden Fight): (1) Without premeditation; (2) In a sudden fight; (3) In the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel; (4) Offender not having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
The incident was spontaneous without premeditation. A single blow was struck in sudden heat. Offender did not take undue advantage. Conviction altered from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I IPC.
Complainant challenged successive bail orders granted by High Court to Pappu Yadav in Ajit Sarkar MLA murder case.

Successive bail applications: While rejection of earlier bail does not bar a fresh application, court must examine whether fresh grounds or changed circumstances exist. Earlier findings on merits cannot be bypassed.
Accused was a powerful politician with criminal history who had previously misused bail by holding political durbars inside jail. High Court bail cancelled.
Constitution Bench resolved conflicting decisions on whether Section 195(1)(b)(ii) CrPC bars private complaint when a forged will is produced in probate court.

Held: The statutory bar under Section 195(1)(b)(ii) CrPC (requiring court complaint for offences against public justice) applies ONLY when the forgery is committed after the document is produced or in the custody of the court (custodia legis).
If the document was forged before it was produced in court, a private criminal complaint under Sections 467/471 IPC is fully maintainable. Private complaint upheld.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Jacob Mathew ... Appellant versus State of Punjab and Another ... Respondents Coram: R.C. Lahoti, C.J., G.P. Mathur, P.K. Balasubramanyan, JJ. Judgment Dated: 05 August 2005 LAHOTI, C.J.: 1. This appeal deals with the legal standard of criminal negligence required to prosecute a medical practitioner under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 for causing death by negligence.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
text: 2. Gross Negligence Requirement: A simple lack of care, an error of judgment or an accident is not sufficient to constitute criminal negligence under Section 304A. In civil law, negligence is actionable on preponderance of probabilities; in criminal law, the negligence must be gross, reckless and amounting to a culpable disregard for human life and safety (mens rea of reckless disregard).

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Jacob Mathew v. State of Punjab and Another
text: 3. Safeguards for Medical Practitioners: To protect medical professionals from malicious or frivolous criminal prosecution, the Supreme Court laid down mandatory guidelines: (1) A private complaint shall not be entertained unless supported by a credible medical expert opinion; (2) An investigating officer shall not arrest a doctor unless gross negligence is established by independent medical testimony.
Deceased died of asphyxia due to pressure on neck within 10 months of marriage after her family failed to fulfill dowry demand of a motorcycle and buffalo.

Ingredients of Dowry Death under Section 304B IPC: (1) Death within seven years of marriage; (2) Occurred by burns, bodily injury, or abnormal circumstances; (3) Woman subjected to cruelty or harassment by husband/in-laws; (4) Cruelty soon before death in connection with dowry demand.
Section 113B of the Evidence Act mandates the court to presume dowry death once these ingredients are established. Accused failed to rebut the presumption. Conviction under Section 304B upheld.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION State (NCT of Delhi) ... Appellant versus Navjot Sandhu @ Afsan Guru and Others ... Respondents Coram: P. Venkatarama Reddi, P.P. Naolekar, JJ. Judgment Dated: 04 August 2005 VENKATARAMA REDDI, J.: 1. This appeal deals with the prosecution of the conspirators of the terrorist attack on the Indian Parliament on 13 December 2001, focusing on charges under Sections 120B, 121 and 302 of the Indian Penal Code.

2. Proof of Criminal Conspiracy (Sections 120A and 120B IPC): The agreement between conspirators is the crux of the offence under Section 120A IPC. Conspiracies are hatched in secrecy, and direct evidence is seldom available. The court can infer criminal conspiracy from surrounding circumstances, conduct of accused before and after the occurrence, frequent telephone communications, and common pursuit of unlawful ends.

3. Decision on Guilt: Mohammed Afzal Guru's active conspiracy with the deceased Pakistani terrorists to wage war against the Government of India and attack Parliament was established beyond reasonable doubt by circumstantial and electronic call record evidence. Death sentence under Section 302 read with Section 120B affirmed.
Accused demanded extortion money ('rangdari tax') from a medical shop owner under threat of demolition of his shop.
Essential ingredients of Extortion under Section 383 IPC: (1) Intentionally putting a person in fear of any injury; (2) Dishonestly inducing the person so put in fear to deliver any property.
If property is not delivered in consequence of fear, offence is not extortion under Section 384, but attempt to commit extortion under Section 385/387 IPC. Conviction sustained.
Discharge application filed by bank officer under Section 227 CrPC in loan fraud chargesheet.

Standard of proof at the stage of framing charges under Sections 227 and 228 CrPC: Court is not required to weigh evidence to see if it would lead to conviction; strong suspicion founded on material is sufficient.
If two views are equally possible and materials show mere grave suspicion without foundational facts, accused is entitled to discharge. Discharge granted.
Company and bank compromised civil dispute before Debts Recovery Tribunal and executed full discharge. Accused sought quashing of CBI chargesheet under Sections 420, 468, 471 IPC.

Supreme Court held: Even though offences under Sections 468 and 471 IPC are non-compoundable, where dispute is predominantly civil/commercial and parties have settled all claims, criminal proceedings should be quashed.
Continuing criminal prosecution after total financial settlement serves no purpose. Chargesheet quashed under Section 482 CrPC.
Father of deceased army officer approached High Court under Section 482 CrPC seeking CBI investigation after police failed to register FIR for murder.
Section 156(3) CrPC gives Magistrate wide powers to ensure proper investigation: Magistrate can order registration of FIR, monitor progress of investigation, and ensure speedy and fair inquiry.
When police refuse to register FIR, the aggrieved party should approach the Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC rather than rushing to High Court under Article 226 or Section 482 CrPC.
Accused executed a registered sale deed conveying land which did not belong to him, claiming to be the owner. Complainant filed FIR under Sections 467, 471 and 420 IPC for forgery.

Supreme Court held: A person who executes a document conveying property falsely claiming to be the owner does not make a 'false document' under Section 464 IPC. A false document requires simulating another person's signature or identity.
Executing a deed without having title is not forgery under Section 463/464. If no false document is made, charges under Section 467 and Section 471 cannot stand. Forgery charges quashed.
In the 1992 securities scam, bank officers fabricated false debit vouchers and credit advices to siphon funds to stockbrokers.

Sections 468 & 471 IPC: To establish forgery, document must be false under Section 464 IPC, made with fraudulent intent. Authorizing false financial entries in official capacity without simulating another identity is not forgery under Section 464.
Forging voucher signatures was proved against specific officers. Conviction under Section 468/471 affirmed for those who created false signatures.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION V.Y. Jose and Another ... Appellants versus State of Gujarat and Another ... Respondents Coram: S.B. Sinha, Cyriac Joseph, JJ. Judgment Dated: 16 December 2008 S.B. SINHA, J.: 1. This appeal highlights the distinction between a commercial default in the supply of machinery and the offence of cheating under Sections 417 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

2. Sections 417 & 418 IPC Principles: Section 417 penalizes simple cheating, whereas Section 418 penalizes cheating where the offender knows that wrongful loss may ensue to a person whose interest he was bound to protect. An essential ingredient for both is the fraudulent or dishonest inducement at the inception. Commercial inability or breach of warranty does not constitute cheating unless dishonest intent existed from the start.

3. Decision: In commercial transactions involving delay in delivery or defects in equipment, criminal proceedings cannot be used as an arm-twisting tool to enforce money recovery. The criminal complaint under Sections 417 and 420 IPC was quashed.
Appellants faced armed assault by complainants over agricultural land. Appellant fired a gun causing death of an aggressor and pleaded right of private defence.

Supreme Court formulated 10 golden principles governing the right of private defence under Sections 96 to 106 IPC: (1) Right is defensive, not retributive; (2) Available only against imminent danger; (3) Cannot weigh force in golden scales; (4) Need not run away when confronted with fatal attack.

The complainant party came armed with deadly weapons and assaulted the appellant. Appellant had reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt under Section 100 IPC. Right of private defence upheld; acquittal granted.
High Court granted bail to murder accused in a single-paragraph unreasoned order. Deceased's father appealed to Supreme Court.

Supreme Court enumerated 7 mandatory factors for bail in heinous crimes: (1) Prima facie case; (2) Nature and gravity of accusation; (3) Severity of punishment; (4) Danger of accused absconding; (5) Character and criminal antecedents; (6) Danger of witness tampering; (7) Larger public interest.
High Court failed to consider heinous nature of murder and witness danger. Mechanical grant of bail set aside.
Married sister-in-law and unmarried brother-in-law living in different cities were roped into an FIR under Section 498A IPC filed by estranged wife.
Supreme Court expressed serious concern over widespread abuse of Section 498A IPC, where general and omnibus allegations are made against distant relatives of husband.
Implicating relatives without specific allegations of harassment or dowry demand is an abuse of process. Criminal proceedings against sister-in-law quashed under Section 482 CrPC.

Constitutionality of non-consensual administration of neuro-scientific investigative techniques: Narco-analysis (truth serum), Polygraph test (lie detector), and Brain Electrical Activation Profile (BEAP).
Supreme Court held: Involuntary administration of narco-analysis or polygraph violates Article 20(3) (Right against self-incrimination) and Article 21 (Right to privacy and mental autonomy).
Results of such involuntary tests are inadmissible as evidence. However, physical evidence or weapons discovered pursuant to voluntary tests are admissible under Section 27 Evidence Act.
Petition filed by next friend on behalf of Aruna Shanbaug, a nurse in a permanent vegetative state for 37 years following sexual assault, seeking withdrawal of life support.
Supreme Court distinguished between active euthanasia (which is illegal homicide under Section 302/304 IPC) and passive euthanasia (withdrawal of life-support systems).

Passive euthanasia permitted under strict safeguards requiring approval of High Court Division Bench after consulting a committee of three expert doctors. Parliament recommended to repeal Section 309 IPC.
Deceased committed suicide alleging she was refused a family car on marriage day. Relatives charged with abetment of suicide under Section 306 IPC.
To convict under Section 306 IPC, there must be a clear mens rea to drive the victim to suicide, coupled with an active act or direct conduct of such nature that the deceased was left with no option.
Hyper-sensitive reactions to domestic incidents cannot be termed abetment. There was no direct nexus between the refusal of the car and the suicide. Proceedings under Section 306 quashed.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO. 8989 OF 2010 GIAN SINGH ... PETITIONER VERSUS STATE OF PUNJAB AND ANOTHER ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT R.M. LODHA, J. 1. The question before this three-Judge Bench is whether the High Court has the power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) to quash criminal proceedings in non-compoundable offences where the parties have settled the dispute amicably.

2. In our considered view, the power of the High Court in quashing a criminal proceeding or FIR under Section 482 of the Code is distinct from the power of a criminal court for compounding the offences under Section 320 of the Code. Inherent power under Section 482 is of wide plenitude with no statutory limitation but must be exercised with circumspection to secure the ends of justice. 3. In cases of offences arising from commercial, financial, mercantile, civil, partnership or such like transactions, or offences arising out of matrimony relating to dowry, etc. or family disputes where the wrong is basically private or personal in nature and the parties have resolved their entire dispute, High Court may quash the criminal proceedings if continuation would be an abuse of process of law.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2178 OF 2011 SANJAY CHANDRA ... APPELLANT VERSUS CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION ... RESPONDENT JUDGMENT H.L. DATTU, J. 1. In the present appeal, the appellants are seeking bail in connection with alleged economic offenses involving cheating under Section 420 and criminal conspiracy under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. 2. The primary question is whether detention in judicial custody pending trial should be used as a punitive measure. The object of bail is neither punitive nor preventive. Deprivation of liberty must be considered a punishment, unless it can be required for ensuring that an accused person will stand his trial when called upon.

3. The grant of bail under Section 439 of the CrPC must balance the gravity of the economic offense with the constitutional guarantee under Article 21. Merely because the offense is of serious nature or involves high financial stakes, the accused cannot be incarcerated indefinitely when the investigation is complete and the charge-sheet has been filed. 4. As observed in State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (1977) 4 SCC 308, the basic rule may perhaps be tersely put as bail, not jail, except where there are circumstances suggestive of fleeing from justice or repeating offenses.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Rishi Pal v. State of Uttarakhand
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Rishi Pal ... Appellant versus State of Uttarakhand ... Respondent Coram: T.S. Thakur, Gyan Sudha Misra, JJ. Judgment Dated: 08 February 2013 THAKUR, J.: 1. This appeal examines the distinction between simple theft under Section 379, theft with preparation for causing death or hurt under Section 382, and robbery under Section 390/392 of the Indian Penal Code.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Rishi Pal v. State of Uttarakhand
text: 2. Ingredients of Section 382 IPC: Section 382 provides rigorous punishment up to ten years where the offender commits theft having made preparation for causing death, hurt, or restraint, or fear of death, hurt or restraint, in order to the committing of such theft, or in order to effect his escape after committing theft, or in order to retain property taken by theft.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Rishi Pal v. State of Uttarakhand
text: 3. Decision: The carrying of concealed weapons (knives, firearms) by the thieves during the nocturnal raid on the warehouse established preparation to cause hurt if intercepted. Conviction under Section 382 IPC affirmed.
Accused made a voluntary judicial confession under Section 164 CrPC admitting murder of his brother, and subsequently retracted it during trial.
Supreme Court on Retracted Confession: A confession recorded in compliance with Section 164 CrPC does not lose its evidentiary value merely because it is retracted at the trial.

If the court is satisfied that the confession was voluntary and truthful, a conviction can be sustained, provided there is general corroboration on material particulars. Conviction under Section 302 affirmed.
Appellants sentenced to death for multiple murders. Supreme Court reviewed inconsistency and subjectivity in death penalty sentencing post-Bachan Singh.
Held: Balancing of aggravating and mitigating circumstances has become judge-centric rather than objective. Courts have frequently ignored the possibility of reformation of the convict.
Death penalty commuted to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 20 years without remission.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Criminal Appeal No. 1277 of 2014 Arnesh Kumar ... Appellant versus State of Bihar and Another ... Respondents Coram: Chandramauli Kr. Prasad and Pinaki Chandra Ghose, JJ. Judgment Dated: 02 July, 2014 CHANDRAMAULI KR. PRASAD, J.: 1. The petitioner apprehending arrest in a case registered under Section 498-A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 had approached this Court for grant of anticipatory bail after his prayer was rejected by the High Court of Patna.

5. Arrest brings humiliation, curtails freedom and casts scars forever. No arrest can be made in a mechanical manner merely because the allegation pertains to a cognizable offence. Section 41 of the Code of Criminal Procedure clearly stipulates the conditions precedent before an arrest can be effected without warrant for offences carrying imprisonment up to seven years. 6. The police officer must satisfy himself about the necessity of arrest based on parameters specified in Section 41(1)(b) CrPC: to prevent the person from committing any further offence, for proper investigation, or to prevent tampering with evidence.

11. We direct that in all cases where offences are punishable with imprisonment for a term which may be less than seven years or which may extend to seven years, whether with or without fine: (1) Police officers shall not arrest the accused unnecessarily without satisfying the checklist under Section 41(1)(b) CrPC. (2) Notice of appearance in terms of Section 41A CrPC shall be served on the accused within two weeks from the date of institution of the case. (3) Failure to comply with these directions shall render police officers liable for departmental action and contempt of court.
Editors of Ananda Bazar Patrika published a nude photograph of tennis star Boris Becker with his dark-skinned fiancée celebrating love against apartheid, and were charged under Section 292 IPC.

Supreme Court formally discarded the outdated Hicklin test and adopted the 'contemporary community standards test': A picture or writing is obscene only if viewed as a whole, it appeals to prurient interest with lascivious purpose.
Nudity per se does not constitute obscenity. The photograph conveyed an anti-racism message and did not arouse lascivious thoughts. Proceedings under Section 292 IPC quashed.
Constitution Bench examined whether Court of Session has power under Section 193 CrPC to summon persons not named in police chargesheet without waiting for evidence under Section 319.
Held: Upon committal of case under Section 209 CrPC, the Court of Session takes cognizance of the entire offence as a court of original jurisdiction under Section 193 CrPC.
Court of Session can summon additional accused shown in column 2 of chargesheet at the stage of framing charges, without waiting for witness evidence under Section 319 CrPC.
Constitution Bench settled the scope and standard of evidence required to summon additional persons as accused under Section 319 CrPC during trial.

Held: The word 'evidence' in Section 319 CrPC means statement of witnesses recorded during trial examination-in-chief, even before cross-examination. Power can be exercised against persons not named in FIR or discharged.
The degree of satisfaction required is more than a prima facie case at charge stage, but less than proof beyond reasonable doubt: reasonable satisfaction that accused committed the offence.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 68 OF 2008 LALITA KUMARI ... PETITIONER VERSUS GOVT. OF U.P. & ORS. ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT P. SATHASIVAM, CJI. 1. The important legal question referred to this Constitution Bench is whether a police officer is bound to register a First Information Report (FIR) upon receiving information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) or whether the police officer has the power to conduct a preliminary inquiry before registering the FIR.

2. In view of the clear legislative mandate of Section 154(1) of the Code, registration of FIR is mandatory if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation. 3. If the information received does not disclose a cognizable offence but indicates the necessity for an inquiry, a preliminary inquiry may be conducted only to ascertain whether cognizable offence is disclosed or not. Such cases may include matrimonial disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence cases, corruption cases, or cases where there is abnormal delay in reporting. 4. The preliminary inquiry must be completed expeditiously and in any case within 7 days. The police officer cannot avoid his duty of registering an offence if cognizable offence is made out.
Public Interest Litigation by acid attack survivor Laxmi seeking total ban on over-the-counter sale of acid and rehabilitation for acid attack victims.

Supreme Court issued nationwide mandatory directives: (1) Over-the-counter sale of acid banned without photo ID and register; (2) Minimum victim compensation of Rs. 3 lakhs under Section 357A CrPC; (3) Free medical treatment at all government and private hospitals under Section 357C CrPC.

Affirmed severity of punishment under Section 326A (Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by acid, minimum 10 years up to life) and Section 326B (Attempt to throw acid) enacted via Criminal Law Amendment Act, 2013.
PIL seeking directions to curb hate speeches delivered by political leaders during election campaigns targeting migrant communities.

Supreme Court held: Existing statutory provisions under Sections 153A, 153B, 295A and 505 IPC and Section 123(3) RPA are sufficient to tackle hate speech if strictly enforced by law enforcement agencies.
Law Commission of India requested to examine whether further specific legal definitions are required for hate speech. Directed election authorities to enforce model code of conduct rigorously.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 167 OF 2012 SHREYA SINGHAL ... PETITIONER VERSUS UNION OF INDIA ... RESPONDENT JUDGMENT R.F. NARIMAN, J. 1. This batch of writ petitions raises questions of great constitutional importance touching upon the fundamental right of free speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India. The primary challenge is directed against Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

2. Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 penalizes the sending of offensive messages through communication services. We find that the terms used in Section 66A such as 'offensive' and 'annoyance' are vague, nebulous, and lack clear judicial definition, creating an impermissible chilling effect on speech. 3. Consequently, Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is declared unconstitutional in its entirety as being violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved under Article 19(2). However, provisions dealing with cyber offenses, identity theft under Section 66C, and cheating by personation under Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 remain valid and enforceable.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION Dr. Subramanian Swamy ... Petitioner versus Union of India, Ministry of Law and Others ... Respondents Coram: Dipak Misra, Prafulla C. Pant, JJ. Judgment Dated: 13 May 2016 DIPAK MISRA, J.: 1. The constitutional validity of Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 providing for criminal defamation is challenged as violating the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

2. Balance Between Free Speech and Right to Reputation: Reputation is an integral constituent of the right to life with dignity under Article 21 of the Constitution. Article 19(2) expressly permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in relation to 'defamation'. Defamation as a penal offence under Section 499 is not disproportionate or arbitrary.

3. Decision: The ten exceptions provided under Section 499 IPC (including truth for public good, fair criticism of public servants, and opinions expressed in good faith) provide adequate safeguards against vexatious prosecutions. Sections 499 and 500 IPC are constitutionally valid. Petitions dismissed.
Constitutional challenge to Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC, which decriminalized sexual intercourse by a man with his wife being not under 15 years of age.
Exception 2 conflicted with POCSO Act (which defines child as under 18) and Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, violating bodily integrity of minor girl children under Articles 14, 15 and 21.
Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC read down: Sexual intercourse with a girl child below 18 years of age, even if she is married, constitutes rape under Section 375/376 IPC.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Mukesh, Pawan Gupta, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Kumar Singh ... Appellants versus State for NCT of Delhi ... Respondent Coram: Dipak Misra, R. Banumathi, Ashok Bhushan, JJ. Judgment Dated: 05 May 2017 DIPAK MISRA, J.: 1. The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death for offences under Section 302, Section 376(2)(g) / Section 376D, Section 365, Section 397 read with Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code arising from the brutal gang-rape and fatal torture of a 23-year-old paramedical student in a moving bus in Delhi on 16 December 2012.

2. Forensic Evidence and Dying Declaration: The prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt through DNA profiling matching the accused to the victim and the crime scene, odontology bite mark analysis, electronic call records, and three consistent dying declarations of the victim.

3. Aggravating Factors and Death Sentence: The unprecedented barbaric and demonic manner in which the offences of gang rape and murder were executed shattered the social fabric and shocked the collective conscience of the nation. The crime falls squarely within the category of 'rarest of rare cases' warranting confirmation of the death penalty under Section 302 and Section 376D IPC.
Accused charged with extortion, land grabbing and cheating sought quashing of criminal proceedings under Section 482 CrPC on basis of compromise with victims.

Supreme Court formulated 10 comprehensive guidelines on quashing under Section 482 on compromise: Heinous and serious offences (rape, murder, dacoity, economic offences against society) cannot be quashed on private settlement.
Accused had 17 criminal cases of extortion and organized land grabbing. Inherent powers under Section 482 cannot be exercised to facilitate extortion compromises. Quashing denied.
9-Judge Constitution Bench examined whether the Right to Privacy is a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution.
Unanimously held: The Right to Privacy is a fundamental right protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed by Part III.
Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962). Informational privacy, bodily privacy, and spatial privacy recognized as constitutional values.
Constitution Bench recognized the right to die with dignity as a fundamental right under Article 21, legalizing 'Advance Medical Directives' (Living Will) and passive euthanasia.
A person with capacity has the right to refuse medical treatment or life-support systems when facing terminal illness with no hope of recovery.
Supreme Court laid down comprehensive guidelines for execution and revocation of Living Wills and authentication by medical boards.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 227 OF 2018 DATARAM SINGH ... APPELLANT VERSUS STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH & ANR. ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT DEEPAK GUPTA, J. 1. A fundamental postulate of criminal jurisprudence is the presumption of innocence, meaning thereby that a person is believed to be innocent until found guilty. Freedom of an individual is of utmost importance in our constitutional governance, enshrined under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

2. It is a well-settled principle of criminal law that bail is the rule and committal to jail is an exception. The grant of bail is an exercise of judicial discretion under Section 437 and Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC). The discretion must be exercised judiciously and not arbitrarily or mechanically. 3. The conditions for grant of bail must not be onerous or unreasonable so as to render the grant illusory. The court must examine whether the accused is likely to flee from justice, tamper with evidence, or influence witnesses.
Constitution Bench challenge to the validity of Section 497 IPC (Adultery) which penalized only the adulterous man and treated women as property of husbands.
Section 497 violated Articles 14, 15 and 21 of the Constitution by discriminating against women, denying sexual autonomy, and enforcing patriarchal notions.
Section 497 IPC and Section 198(2) CrPC struck down as unconstitutional. Adultery remains a ground for civil divorce but is no longer a criminal offence.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CONSTITUTION BENCH
Navtej Singh Johar and Others v. Union of India
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CONSTITUTION BENCH Navtej Singh Johar and Others ... Petitioners versus Union of India ... Respondent Coram: Dipak Misra, C.J., R.F. Nariman, A.M. Khanwilkar, D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra, JJ. Judgment Dated: 06 September 2018 DIPAK MISRA, C.J.: 1. The petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 in so far as it criminalises consensual carnal intercourse against the order of nature between consenting adults in private.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CONSTITUTION BENCH
Navtej Singh Johar and Others v. Union of India
text: 2. Constitutional Morality over Majoritarian Morality: Sexual orientation is an innate aspect of individual privacy, dignity and personal autonomy protected under Articles 14, 19(1)(a) and 21 of the Constitution. Constitutional morality must trump social morality.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CONSTITUTION BENCH
Navtej Singh Johar and Others v. Union of India
text: 3. Decision: Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code is unconstitutional to the extent it penalises consensual sexual relations between consenting adults in private. Non-consensual carnal intercourse and sexual offences against minors or animals continue to remain governed by Section 377 IPC and relevant penal statutes.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj and Another
text: IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Sheila Sebastian ... Appellant versus R. Jawaharaj and Another ... Respondents Coram: N.V. Ramana, S. Abdul Nazeer, JJ. Judgment Dated: 11 May 2018 RAMANA, J.: 1. This criminal appeal involves the definition of forgery under Section 463 and 'making a false document' under Section 464 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 in relation to an allegedly forged power of attorney.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj and Another
text: 2. Making of False Document is Sine Qua Non for Forgery: The essential ingredient of forgery under Section 463 is the making of a false document as defined under Section 464 IPC. Unless the accused is proved to have forged the signature or made the document, or caused someone else to make it, he cannot be convicted of forgery under Section 465 or Section 468 IPC.

case_name:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj and Another
text: 3. Decision: The prosecution failed to establish that respondent Jawaharaj made or signed the forged power of attorney, although it was registered in his favour. An accused cannot be convicted of forgery simply because he is the beneficiary of a forged document, unless he is shown to be the author or conspirator. Acquittal under Section 468 IPC upheld.
Accused was granted bail in a case; during investigation, police added grave non-bailable offences under Section 302 IPC and UAPA, and arrested accused without bail cancellation.

Supreme Court settled procedure when serious non-bailable offences are added: Investigating officer cannot straightaway arrest accused who is already on bail; police must apply to court for cancellation or surrender.
Court has power to direct accused to surrender and apply for fresh bail in respect of newly added aggravated offences.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Criminal Appeal No. 1340 of 2019 P. Chidambaram ... Appellant versus Directorate of Enforcement ... Respondent Coram: R. Banumathi and A.S. Bopanna, JJ. Judgment Dated: 05 September, 2019 R. BANUMATHI, J.: 1. This appeal arises out of the order passed by the High Court of Delhi refusing to grant anticipatory bail to the appellant in respect of offences alleged under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

19. The grant of anticipatory bail in economic offences stands on a different footing. Economic offences have deep-rooted conspiracies involving huge loss of public funds. Anticipatory bail is not to be granted as a matter of rule in cases where custodial interrogation of the accused is necessary to unearth the money trail and unravel complex illicit transactions. 20. The discretion under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is extraordinary in character and must be exercised with caution, particularly where granting protection may impede a fair and effective investigation.
Complaint filed under Section 420 IPC alleging cheating in respect of an agreement to purchase an apartment after civil suit was already instituted.

Supreme Court held: A breach of contract does not give rise to criminal cheating unless fraudulent intention is shown at the inception of the contract. Criminal courts cannot be used to exert pressure for civil debt recovery.
Allowing criminal proceedings where allegations are essentially civil in nature constitutes an abuse of the judicial process. Complaint under Section 420 IPC quashed under Section 482 CrPC.
Complaint filed alleging accused came to complainant's house, abused him in filthy language, and threatened him over unpaid debt.

Section 503 defines Criminal Intimidation; Section 506 punishes it. Mere expression of words of abuse without intent to cause alarm or threat to cause injury does not constitute criminal intimidation.
Vituperative language used in anger without real threat to person or reputation does not satisfy Section 506 IPC. Criminal proceedings quashed.
Challenge to prolonged indefinite internet shutdown and movement restrictions in Jammu & Kashmir under Section 144 CrPC post-abrogation of Article 370.

Supreme Court held: Freedom of speech and trade over the internet is constitutionally protected under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g). Section 144 CrPC cannot be used as a tool to suppress legitimate expression of democratic grievances.
Orders under Section 144 CrPC must state material facts, satisfy the proportionality test, and be published. Indefinite suspension of internet services held impermissible.
Three-Judge Bench settled conflicting precedents on admissibility of electronic evidence (CDs, CCTV footage, mobile printouts) under Section 65B Evidence Act.
Certificate under Section 65B(4) is an absolute condition precedent for admissibility of secondary electronic evidence. Overruled Shafhi Mohammad (2018); affirmed Anvar P.V. (2014).

Where party is not in possession of the electronic device, application can be made to court under Section 165 Evidence Act / Order XVI CPC to compel production of 65B certificate from the device custodian.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Criminal Appeal No. 707 of 2020 Hitesh Verma ... Appellant versus State of Uttarakhand and Another ... Respondents Coram: L. Nageswara Rao, Hemant Gupta and Ajay Rastogi, JJ. Judgment Dated: 05 November, 2020 HEMANT GUPTA, J.: 1. The challenge in the present appeal is to an order passed by the High Court of Uttarakhand dismissing an application filed by the appellant under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for quashing of the charge-sheet and summoning order in respect of offences punishable under Sections 504 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

11. The basic ingredients of an offence under Section 504 IPC are that there must be an intentional insult and it must give provocation to any person intending or knowing that it is likely to break the public peace. In the absence of any allegation of public view, the offence cannot be sustained. 18. The inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is intended to prevent the abuse of the process of any court and to secure the ends of justice. Where the allegations in the FIR and charge-sheet do not disclose the commission of any cognizable offence, continuation of criminal proceedings constitutes harassment.
High Court granted bail to a murder accused with 14 criminal antecedents in a perfunctory order recording only 'without expressing any opinion on the merits of the case'.

Chandrachud J. on Duty to Give Reasons in Bail: While court is not required to conduct a mini-trial, it must indicate its reasoning demonstrating application of mind to nature of crime, criminal antecedents, and witness threat.
An unreasoned bail order in a heinous murder case suffers from non-application of mind and perversity. High Court order set aside; bail cancelled.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Special Leave Petition (Crl.) Nos. 7281-7282 of 2017 Sushila Aggarwal and Others ... Petitioners versus State (NCT of Delhi) and Another ... Respondents Coram: Arun Mishra, Indira Banerjee, Vineet Saran, M.R. Shah and S. Ravindra Bhat, JJ. Judgment Dated: 29 January, 2020 M.R. SHAH, J. and S. RAVINDRA BHAT, J. (Concurring): 1. The reference to this Constitution Bench was necessitated due to conflicting views on two vital questions concerning the scope of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973: (1) Whether the protection granted to a person under Section 438 CrPC should be limited to a fixed period so as to enable the person to surrender before the trial court and seek regular bail; (2) Whether the life of an anticipatory bail order ends at the time and stage when the accused is summoned by the court.

27. In Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 565, the Constitution Bench of this Court categorically held that Section 438 CrPC is a procedural provision guaranteeing personal liberty under Article 21. The Court in Sibbia firmly rejected the notion that anticipatory bail orders should be made for a limited time span as a matter of inflexible rule. 28. We are in respectful agreement with the ruling in Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia. The judgments in Salauddin Abdulsamad Shaikh v. State of Maharashtra (1996) 1 SCC 667 and Mhetre (2011) which laid down restrictive rules contrary to Sibbia do not lay down the correct law.

92. Our final conclusions on the reference are as follows: (1) The protection granted to a person under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should not be invariably limited to a fixed period. In normal circumstances, the protection continues till the end of the trial. (2) The life or duration of an anticipatory bail order does not automatically end or expire upon the filing of the charge-sheet or police report under Section 173(2) CrPC. (3) However, depending upon the special features of a particular case or offences involving custodial interrogation or recovery of articles, the court may impose conditions or restrict the duration of anticipatory bail if warranted.
Television journalist aired debate referring to Sufi saint Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti in derogatory terms. Multiple FIRs filed under Sections 153A, 295A and 505(2) IPC.

Supreme Court expounded on Hate Speech: Differentiated between 'free speech' (which can be hurtful or provocative) and 'hate speech' (which targets identity of a community with intent to promote hatred or marginalization).
Refused to quash FIRs under Section 482; journalist's intent and impact of broadcast required police investigation. Consolidated all FIRs to one police station.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 330 OF 2021 M/S NEEHARIKA INFRASTRUCTURE PVT. LTD. ... APPELLANT VERSUS STATE OF MAHARASHTRA AND OTHERS ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT M.R. SHAH, J. 1. The core issue before this three-Judge Bench relates to the scope and power of the High Court under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) and Article 226 of the Constitution of India in passing interim orders of 'no coercive steps' or staying arrest during the pendency of quashing petitions.

2. Police have the statutory right and duty under Section 156 and relevant provisions of the Code to investigate into a cognizable offence. The courts should not thwart any lawful investigation into cognizable offences. 3. An interim order staying investigation or directing that no coercive steps be taken should be passed only in exceptional cases where the FIR does not disclose any cognizable offence. In petitions under Section 482 CrPC, High Courts should not pass blanket interim orders staying arrest or investigation without recording cogent reasons.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION Satbir Singh and Another ... Appellants versus State of Haryana ... Respondent Coram: N.V. Ramana, C.J., Surya Kant, Aniruddha Bose, JJ. Judgment Dated: 28 May 2021 N.V. RAMANA, C.J.: 1. This judgment sets out comprehensive guidelines for trial courts trying offences under Section 304B (Dowry death) and Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 read with the presumption under Section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

2. Interpretation of 'Soon Before Her Death': The phrase 'soon before her death' in Section 304B IPC cannot be restricted to mean 'immediately before'. It indicates a flexible concept denoting a proximate and live link between the cruelty or harassment related to dowry demands and the unnatural death of the woman within seven years of marriage.

3. Evidentiary Burden and Section 313 CrPC: Once the prosecution proves that the woman died an unnatural death within seven years of marriage and was subjected to dowry cruelty soon before death, Section 113B of the Evidence Act mandates a statutory presumption of dowry death. The trial court must carefully examine the accused under Section 313 CrPC to allow him an opportunity to rebut the presumption.
Wife filed criminal complaint under Section 498A IPC against husband's mother, sisters and brothers alleging demand of car and torture.
Supreme Court held: In matrimonial disputes, relatives cannot be subjected to criminal trial on the basis of general, vague and omnibus allegations without specific dates or overt acts.
To prosecute under Section 498A, there must be clear prima facie evidence of physical or mental cruelty. Proceedings against in-laws quashed under Section 482 CrPC.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO. 5191 OF 2021 SATENDER KUMAR ANTIL ... APPELLANT VERSUS CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION & ANR. ... RESPONDENTS JUDGMENT M.M. SUNDRESH, J. 1. Liberty is one of the most essential facets of our constitutional democracy. The right to personal liberty guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India is inviolable and cannot be curtailed except according to procedure established by law. The primary question before this Court pertains to the categorization of offences and the guidelines governing the grant of regular and anticipatory bail under Sections 436, 437, 438, and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC).

2. In our considered view, undertrial prisoners constitute an overwhelming majority of inmates in Indian prisons. Unwarranted arrests violate the mandate of Section 41 and Section 41A of the CrPC, as enunciated by this Court in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) 8 SCC 273. 3. We lay down four distinct categories of offences for streamline bail processing: - Category A: Offences punishable with imprisonment up to 7 years. Ordinary summons and bailable procedures must be followed without unnecessary arrest. - Category B: Offences punishable with death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for more than 7 years. Bail applications to be decided on merits. - Category C: Offences under Special Acts like NDPS, PMLA, UAPA, containing twin conditions on bail. - Category D: Economic offences not covered by Special Acts, where gravity of offence is balanced with the individual's liberty. 4. We reiterate that Section 88, Section 170, and Section 204 of the CrPC must be strictly adhered to by trial courts to avoid mechanical remands.

5. Compliance with Section 41A of the CrPC is mandatory. The investigating agencies and police officers are required to issue notices of appearance before affecting arrest in offences where imprisonment is up to seven years. Failure to comply with Section 41 and 41A must result in disciplinary action against the erring officers, and the accused shall be entitled to bail. 6. The principle that 'bail is the rule and jail is an exception' as held in Dataram Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2018) 3 SCC 22 must remain the guiding light for all criminal courts in the country. The applications for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC and regular bail under Section 439 CrPC should be disposed of expeditiously, normally within two weeks.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 3387 OF 2023 MANISH SISODIA ... APPELLANT VERSUS CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION ... RESPONDENT JUDGMENT SANJIV KHANNA, J. 1. The appellant seeks regular bail under Section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC) in cases investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Directorate of Enforcement (ED) concerning the Delhi Excise Policy. 2. Right to speedy trial is a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. In cases where the trial gets delayed and incarceration extends beyond a reasonable period, the constitutional court is empowered to grant bail even in matters involving stringent statutory conditions.

3. Prolonged pre-trial detention without commencement or conclusion of trial cannot become punitive. If the trial cannot proceed with reasonable dispatch, the accused is entitled to renew the prayer for bail under Section 439 CrPC.
Supreme Court issued mandatory guidelines for trial courts conducting sentencing hearings in death penalty cases under Section 235(2) CrPC.
Mandated collection of psychiatric and psychological evaluation of the accused, report from jail authorities on conduct and vocational work, and socio-economic background report prior to sentencing.
Sentencing hearing cannot be conducted on the same day as conviction. Trial courts must afford meaningful opportunity for defense to lead mitigating evidence.
Investigating agencies filed incomplete chargesheets (without FSL/investigation completion) to prevent accused from seeking statutory default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC.
Right to default bail under Section 167(2) CrPC is a fundamental right emanating from Article 21. An incomplete investigation report does not defeat default bail.
Filing piecemeal chargesheet without completing investigation violates statutory mandate. Accused is entitled to default bail if full investigation is not concluded within prescribed 60/90 days.
Criminal proceedings initiated under Section 420 IPC alleging dishonest inducement in securing school admission and fee remittance.
Supreme Court reiterated: Dishonest inducement is the backbone of cheating under Section 415/420 IPC. The complainant must demonstrate deceit which induced delivery of property.
In the absence of deception practiced at the beginning of the transaction, criminal prosecution is untenable. Proceedings quashed.

REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 167 OF 2012 SHREYA SINGHAL ... PETITIONER VERSUS UNION OF INDIA ... RESPONDENT JUDGMENT R.F. NARIMAN, J. 1. This batch of writ petitions raises questions of great constitutional importance touching upon the fundamental right of free speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India. The primary challenge is directed against Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

2. Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 penalizes the sending of offensive messages through communication services. We find that the terms used in Section 66A such as 'offensive' and 'annoyance' are vague, nebulous, and lack clear judicial definition, creating an impermissible chilling effect on speech. 3. Consequently, Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 is declared unconstitutional in its entirety as being violative of Article 19(1)(a) and not saved under Article 19(2). However, provisions dealing with cyber offenses, identity theft under Section 66C, and cheating by personation under Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 remain valid and enforceable.

SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NOS. 7281-7282 OF 2017 Sushila Aggarwal and Others ... Petitioners versus State (NCT of Delhi) and Another ... Respondents Coram: Arun Mishra, Indira Banerjee, Vineet Saran, M.R. Shah, and S. Ravindra Bhat, JJ. Judgment Dated: 29 January, 2020 JUDGMENT 1. The primary issue before this Constitution Bench relates to the scope and ambit of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Specifically, whether the protection granted to a person through anticipatory bail should be invariably limited to a fixed duration so as to compel the accused to surrender before the regular court. 2. In the landmark decision of Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980) 2 SCC 565, this Court ruled that Section 438 CrPC confers wide discretionary powers on the High Court and Sessions Court to safeguard personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.

3. We have carefully examined the rival contentions advanced by the learned Senior Counsel. It was argued on behalf of the prosecution that unbridled anticipatory bail hinders effective investigation under Section 173(2) CrPC. 4. In our considered view, an arbitrary curtailment of liberty through premature cancellation or artificial time limitations undermines the legislative purpose behind enacting Section 438 of the Code. 5. Therefore, as held in Sibbia, the grant of anticipatory bail is not an extraordinary exception to be guarded with suspicion, but a vital guarantee of human dignity and liberty.

OPERATIVE ORDER 92. We answer the reference as follows: (a) Protection granted under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure should not be invariably limited to a fixed period. In normal circumstances, the protection continues till the end of the trial. (b) The life of an order granting anticipatory bail does not automatically expire upon the filing of the charge-sheet or summoning by the court. (c) The Court may impose restrictive conditions in appropriate cases where custodial interrogation is demonstrably essential.
